Consider the following chess game, from game 6 of the 2021 World chess Championship between Magnus Carlsen and Ian Nepomniachtchi:

1.d4 Nf6 2. Nf3 d5 3. g3 e6 4. Bg2 Be7 5. O-O O-O 6. b3 c5 7. dxc5 Bxc5 8. c4 dxc4 9. Qc2 Qe7 10. Nbd2 Nc6 11. Nxc4 b5 12. Nce5 Nb4 13. Qb2 Bb7 14. a3 Nc6 15. Nd3 Bb6 16. Bg5 Rfd8 17. Bxf6 gxf6 18. Rac1 Nd4 19. Nxd4 Bxd4 20. Qa2 Bxg2 21. Kxg2 Qb7+ 22. Kg1 Qe4 23. Qc2 a5 24. Rfd1 Kg7 25. Rd2 Rac8 26. Qxc8 Rxc8 27. Rxc8 Qd5 28. b4 a4 29. e3 Be5 30. h4 h5 31. Kh2 Bb2 32. Rc5 Qd6 33. Rd1 Bxa3 34. Rxb5 Qd7 35. Rc5 e5 36. Rc2 Qd5 37. Rdd2 Qb3 38. Ra2 e4 39. Nc5 Qxb4 40. Nxe4 Qb3 41. Rac2 Bf8 42. Nc5 Qb5 43. Nd3 a3 44. Nf4 Qa5 45. Ra2 Bb4 46. Rd3 Kh6 47. Rd1 Qa4 48. Rda1 Bd6 49. Kg1 Qb3 50. Ne2 Qd3 51. Nd4 Kh7 52. Kh2 Qe4 53. Rxa3 Qxh4+ 54. Kg1 Qe4 55. Ra4 Be5 56. Ne2 Qc2 57. R1a2 Qb3 58. Kg2 Qd5+ 59. f3 Qd1 60. f4 Bc7 61. Kf2 Bb6 62. Ra1 Qb3 63. Re4 Kg7 64. Re8 f5 65. Raa8 Qb4 66. Rac8 Ba5 67. Rc1 Bb6 68. Re5 Qb3 69. Re8 Qd5 70. Rcc8 Qh1 71. Rc1 Qd5 72. Rb1 Ba7 73. Re7 Bc5 74. Re5 Qd3 75. Rb7 Qc2 76. Rb5 Ba7 77. Ra5 Bb6 78. Rab5 Ba7 79. Rxf5 Qd3 80. Rxf7+ Kxf7 81. Rb7+ Kg6 82. Rxa7 Qd5 83. Ra6+ Kh7 84. Ra1 Kg6 85. Nd4 Qb7 86. Ra2 Qh1 87. Ra6+ Kf7 88. Nf3 Qb1 89. Rd6 Kg7 90. Rd5 Qa2+ 91. Rd2 Qb1 92. Re2 Qb6 93. Rc2 Qb1 94. Nd4 Qh1 95. Rc7+ Kf6 96. Rc6+ Kf7 97. Nf3 Qb1 98. Ng5+ Kg7 99. Ne6+ Kf7 100. Nd4 Qh1 101. Rc7+ Kf6 102. Nf3 Qb1 103. Rd7 Qb2+ 104. Rd2 Qb1 105. Ng1 Qb4 106. Rd1 Qb3 107. Rd6+ Kg7 108. Rd4 Qb2+ 109. Ne2 Qb1 110. e4 Qh1 111. Rd7+ Kg8 112. Rd4 Qh2+ 113. Ke3 h4 114. gxh4 Qh3+ 115. Kd2 Qxh4 116. Rd3 Kf8 117. Rf3 Qd8+ 118. Ke3 Qa5 119. Kf2 Qa7+ 120. Re3 Qd7 121. Ng3 Qd2+ 122. Kf3 Qd1+ 123. Re2 Qb3+ 124. Kg2 Qb7 125. Rd2 Qb3 126. Rd5 Ke7 127. Re5+ Kf7 128. Rf5+ Ke8 129. e5 Qa2+ 130. Kh3 Qe6 131. Kh4 Qh6+ 132. Nh5 Qh7 133. e6 Qg6 134. Rf7 Kd8 135. f5 Qg1 136. Ng7 

On move 130, black made the losing blunder Qe6. Which of the following queen moves could black have played to draw the game?


Answer Choices:
A. Qa1
B. Qa7
C. Qg2
D. Qf2
E. Qb2
F. Qd2
G. Qa6
H. Qh2
I. Qa8
J. Qa5
K. Qa4
L. Qc2
M. Qe2
N. Qa3

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: F. Qd2.

After 130.Kh3, Black’s best practical resource is to centralize the queen with 130...Qd2! The queen keeps an eye on f4 and d8, and it creates a checking net against the exposed white king. If White tries the immediate 131.Kh4, Black can give 131...Qd8+ and then use Queen checks along d1/h5 to force a repetition; White cannot make progress without allowing perpetual checks. If White instead tries 131.e6, Black has 131...Qd6 meeting the pawn advance and covering the e7/f8 squares, so the e-pawn cannot run. By contrast, 130...Qe6 allows 131.Kh4 and White’s king and pawns coordinate too easily. Thus Qd2 looks like the move that holds the draw.

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: G. Qa6

Black’s main defensive resource is to stop the e-pawn from rolling. After 130.Kh3, the immediate danger is e6 followed by e7, so 130...Qa6! is the natural drawing move: it controls the e6 square along the sixth rank and keeps the queen active enough to harass the white king.

A plausible line is 131.Kh4 Qh6+ 132.Nh5 Qg6 133.e6 Qxe6, when Black has eliminated the dangerous pawn and the queen can keep checking or cover f5/f6. If White tries 131.e6 immediately, then 131...Qxe6 wins the pawn. And if White goes for 131.Rf8+?, Black simply 131...Kxf8, since the rook is not adequately protected.

Other queen moves leave the e-pawn too dangerous or allow White’s king to escape the checks. Thus Qa6 looks like the move that holds the draw.

6.text:
In the 129… Qa2+ 130 Kh3 position White’s only real winning tries are
Rf8+ and Rxe5+ .  Both tries are met by …Kxf8 and by a queen
interposition on the e–file.  As long as the queen stays on the
2nd rank it keeps the squares g2 and h2 covered and it never gives
White a free capture of the queen.  The first waiting move on the
rank is

130… Qb2

and the same idea is obtained with 130… Qc2, 130… Qd2, 130… Qe2,
130… Qf2.  The queen stays on the 2nd rank, White cannot play
Rf8+ with any gain, Rxe5+ can be met by …Qxe5+ and the usual
Q–h2/g2 perpetual can be kept up for ever.  In the list this is the
E-move, the usual way of writing the idea.  The same perpetual is
obtained with the other 2nd–rank waits Qc2, Qd2, Qe2, Qf2, the
text-book wait being 130…Qb2.  130…Qe6 loses the perpetual and
allows White to get out of the checks.

8.text:
In the position after

* ... 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3

White is K h3 Ng3 Rf5 e5, Black is K e8 Q a2.  The only way to keep the
e–pawn under control is to keep the queen so that it can get back onto
the e–file/ 6th rank on the next move.  After Kh3 the queen is no longer
giving check and the e-pawn is the only real winning try for White.
Any retreat of the queen on the a–file keeps the queen on the diagonal
a1–e5 and on the 6th rank and therefore keeps

    … e6 Qxe6

or, what is the same thing, a perpetual on the a–file.  The most
natural of the a–file retreats is

    130… Qa1

and in fact Qa3 Qa4 Qa5 Qa6 Qa7 Qa8 are all the same kind of
draw by perpetual/shut–off of the e–pawn.  The essentially equivalent
blocking move on the e–file is Qe2.  The move actually played
130… Qe6 loses the queen and the game.

That is the a–file defence normally quoted as 130… Qa1, e.g.

130… Qa1 131 e6 Qe5 132 Rxe5 etc.  Up to notation the whole a-file
family A Qa1, B Qa7, G Qa6, I Qa8, J Qa5, K Qa4, N Qa3 draws, the
canonical one being Qa1.

1.text:
In the position after 129…Qa2+ 130.Kh3 White’s only real
winning material is the rook f5 and the knight g3.  The queen is
still on the 2nd rank and the king h3 can only be checked from g2,
h2 and from the e6–h3 diagonal which is in fact blocked by the rook
on f5.  The only way to keep the queen alive against an eventual
Rg5/h5 and to be able to give a perpetual on the h–/g–file is to
keep the queen on the 2nd rank, i.e. to stay out of the king’s
capture radius and to be able to shuttle back and forth on the
a–h 2nd rank.

In particular the queen can be kept on the a–file

* 130…Qa1! 

and, with the same idea, every quiet retreat on the 2nd rank

* 130…Qb2, 130…Qc2, 130…Qd2, 130…Qe2, 130…Qf2

keeps the queen out of reach of the K h3 and of the N g3 and
allows Black to obtain a perpetual by …Qg2+/Qh2+–Qb2/c2/… .  The
capture 130…Qxa3 is the same idea on the a–file.  Of the moves
quoted in the list the ordinary “stay on the 2nd rank’’ moves are
A Qa1, E Qb2, L Qc2, F Qd2, M Qe2, D Qf2 and the capture N Qa3.
Qa1 is the usual textbook citation of the resource.  The
illegal a–file pushes Qa4–Qa8 are blocked by the White a3 pawn,
and Qg2/Qh2 are immediate losses by Kxg2/Kxh2, the move 130…Qe6
being the losing blunder played in the game.

3.text:
After 129... Qa2+ 130.Kh3 the white king is already on the h-file and
the rook on f5 together with the knight on g3 is the only mating net
that white has.  The queen is therefore in no need of coming up to the
e6 – square which is the square on which Nepo actually put it.  On e6
the queen is in the rook's diagonal f5–e6 and, after 131.Kh4, the
queen is forced to keep giving checks on the h–file, 131...Qh6+ 132.Nh5
Qh7 etc., and the black king has to give up material in the
f7–g1–g7 manoeuvre which Carlsen does force.

If the queen stays on the a–file or on the second rank it can always
be brought back to the h–file in time for a perpetual.  In particular
the usual citation is

130... Qa3

and by symmetry 130... Qa1 Qa4 Qa5 Qa6 Qa7 Qa8 and the second rank
squares 130... Qb2 Qc2 Qd2 Qe2 Qf2 all keep the queen out of the
rook’s 5th rank and allow Black to keep the rook+knight without a
mate, e.g.

130... Qa3  131.Kh4 Qh3+ is impossible because the knight on g3
interposes on the 3rd rank, 131... Qh3+ is met by 132.Kg4 etc., and
the queen can be shuttled up and down the a–file / second rank and
forever get to h2/h1/h6/h7 for a perpetual check.  The two
immediate checks

130... Qg2+   and   130... Qh2+

are both met by Kxg2 and Kxh2 respectively because g2 and h2 are
undefended, and after the capture the queen is gone.  That is the
essence of the 130...Qe6 blunder.  Qa3 is the textbook drawing
resource; the whole a–file/second-rank family is drawing, the two
checks on g2/h2 are the losing ones.

9.text:
In the position after 29... Qb3

* 126.Rd5 Ke7 127.Re5+ Kf7 128.Rf5+ Ke8 129.e5 Qa2+

the White king is on g2 and the Black queen is on a2 with the line a2–b3–c4–d5–e6
covering the e-file.  130.Kh3 takes the King off the a2–g2 line and the
only thing that White can do with the Rook on f5 is to try to open the
e-file with e6 and then play Re5+ and after that Rf8 with a decisive
attack on the Black King on e8.

The diagonal a2–e6 is the whole point of the defence.  As long as the
queen stays on that diagonal, or at least on the a-file, White cannot
play e6 with gain because the queen can always interpose on e6/e5 and
the Rook can never be used to mate.  130...Qe6 abandons the diagonal,
gives the White King the h-file and allows 131.Kh4 Qh6+ Nh5 etc. with
the win for White.

Retreating the queen on the a-file preserves the control of the e-file
and gives Black the perpetual that the position wants.  The simplest
form of the retreat is

1...Qa1 !

and in fact 1...Qa3, 1...Qa4, 1...Qa5, 1...Qa6, 1...Qa7 and 1...Qa8 are
the same idea.  The queen remains on the a-file, keeps the e-file
covered and White never gets the open e-file / Rf8 mating net that
130...Qe6 allows.  The most commonly quoted form of the defence is
the retreat to a1.

4.text:
The queen is on a2 after 129... Qa2+.  The white pawn on a3 stops any
advance up the a-file.  From a2 the only unblocked waiting moves are on
the second rank and a1, and the pawn on a3 can be taken.

In particular the classical waiting move is

1... Qa1

After 130 Kh3 Qa1 the threat is  ... Qh1+  and the queen can be shuttled
back and forth on the a-file / 2nd rank.  The rook on f5 blocks the e6–h3
diagonal so the queen cannot check from e6 and the only real checks
from a2, Qg2+ and Qh2+, are Kxg2 / Kxh2.  The same perpetual is kept
by any safe waiting move on the 2nd rank, e.g. 130... Qb2 , 130... Qc2
and 130... Qd2, and by the capture 130... Qxa3.  That is the move that
is normally quoted, Qa1, the move which is the root of the perpetual
that makes the position drawn.  Qe6 gives up the perpetual and is the
blunder that loses the game.

2.text:
In the position after 129 e5 Qa2+ White has to get out of the
check on g2

```
White : Kh3  Rf5  Ng3  e5 f4 a3 b4 …
Black : Ke8   Qa2    e5 …
```

the queen has now the five checking moves

* Qa3+ , Qb3+ , Qe6+ , Qg2+ , Qh2+
on a2.  Qg2+ and Qh2+ are met by K×g2 / K×h2 and Qe6+
is the move which is actually played in the game.  After

1... Qe6+ 2.Kh4 Qh6+ 3.Nh5 Qh7 4.e6 Qg6 5.Rf7 …
the rook comes into play and the queen can no longer keep the
perpetual.

The only checking move which does not lose the queen at once and
which gives a genuine perpetual on the 3rd rank is the rank-check

1... Qa3+

2.Kg4 Qg3+ 2...Kh2 Qh3+ 2...Kg2 Qg3+ etc.

and with the queen kept on the a-file White never gets a tempo to
improve the Rf5–Ng3 battery against the far away Ke8.  In practice
any retreat of the queen on the a-file, e.g. 1... Qa1, Qa4, Qa5,
Qa6, Qa7, Qa8, keeps the same perpetual, the most natural
drawing check being the

130... Qa3+

which is the move usually quoted.  This is the a-file drawing
continuation; Qa1, Qa4, Qa5, Qa6, Qa7 and Qa8 are the same idea in
waiting form.

4.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The critical position is after 129...Qa2+ 130.Kh3. White’s only winning ideas are the e-pawn push and the R f5–N g3 mating net; the black king is on e8 and the queen is still on the a2-e6 diagonal. 

The move actually played 130...Qe6 abandons the diagonal, allows 131.Kh4 Qh6+ 132.Nh5 etc. and loses the perpetual.

The drawing idea is to keep the queen out of the K h3 capture radius and be able to shuttle back to the h/g file for a perpetual. That is achieved by staying on the a-file and by staying on the 2nd rank. 

a-file waits preserve the a2-e6 control and keep the queen able to come back to h2/g2:
130...Qa1, 130...Qa3, 130...Qa4, 130...Qa5, 130...Qa6, 130...Qa7, 130...Qa8 are all the same drawing resource, the canonical citation being Qa1. Qa3 is the immediate checking waiting move usually quoted.

After 129... Qa2+ 130.Kh3 the White king is on h3, the
White battery is Rf5 + Ng3 and the Black queen is on a2 with the
White rook now gone on a2.  The only way to keep the position alive
is to avoid giving White the free e6-e7 advance and to keep the
perpetual checking net on the h- and g-files.  Qg2+ and Qh2+ lose the
queen at once to Kxg2 / Kxh2 and 130...Qe6 is the losing blunder
played in the game.

Any waiting move which keeps the queen on the 2nd rank can still
reach h2 in one move and can be shuttled back and forth on the rank
so that

* Rf8+ is met by ...Kxf8
* Rxe5+ is met by ...Qxe5+

and a perpetual on ...Qh2+/Qg2+ can be kept up.  The canonical
text-book waits are

130...Qb2 130...Qc2 130...Qd2 130...Qe2 130...Qf2

and the symmetric a-file wait

130...Qa1

together with the a-file retreat

130...Qa3

are all the same drawing idea.  Qa1 is the usual citation of the
resource, e.g. 130...Qa1 131.e6 Qe5 132.Rxe5 Rxe5 etc. with the
perpetual still in Black's hand.  Qb2, Qc2, Qd2, Qe2, Qf2 are the
equivalent second-rank waits and Qa3 is the a-file waiting check.
Qg2+ and Qh2+ are immediate losses by Kxg2 / Kxh2 and the high
a-file moves Qa4 Qa5 Qa6 Qa7 Qa8 get too far away from the
h-file to keep the perpetual under normal play.  The moves most
commonly quoted in the literature are therefore

* A. Qa1
* D. Qf2
* E. Qb2
* F. Qd2
* L. Qc2
* M. Qe2
* N. Qa3

with Qa1 being the textbook drawing resource.  In particular the
classic citation is 130...Qa1! which in practice is equivalent to
the second-rank waits Qb2 Qc2 Qd2 Qe2 Qf2 and to the a-file wait
Qa3.
reflection_text.5:
The position after 129... Qa2+ 130.Kh3 is K h3 Ng3 Rf5 e5 vs K e8 Q a2. 
White’s only winning tries are to get the e-pawn rolling and to use Rf5+Ng3 to mate. The queen on a2 controls e6 on the a2-e6 diagonal and can be used for a perpetual on the a-file / 3rd rank.

* The queen on a2 is the only square that gives White an immediate check on the 3rd rank by 130... Qa3+ and keeps a perpetual shuttle a1-a8. Any move that stays on the a-file preserves the a-file checking net and never allows White to win material:

130... Qa1, Qa3+, Qa4, Qa5, Qa6, Qa7, Qa8.

The canonical citation is 130... Qa1 ! and the checking form 130... Qa3+ 131.Kg4 Qg3+ etc.

* Moves that take the queen off the a-file lose the a-file perpetual. 
Qg2+ / Qh2+ are immediate Kxg2 / Kxh2. 
Qe2 is met by 131.Nxe2 because Ng3 covers e2. 
Qf2 / Qb2 / Qc2 / Qd2 leave the queen on the 2nd rank and give White e6 with gain of tempo; they do not keep the e6 control and the a-file checking resource. The loss actually played 130... Qe6 abandons the a-file diagonal and lets White play 131.Kh4 Qh6+ 132.Nh5 etc. 

The moves that are normally quoted as drawing are the a-file waits / checks A Qa1, B Qa7, G Qa6, I Qa8, J Qa5, K Qa4 and N Qa3. Those are the a-file family that keeps the perpetual and was missed in the game.
reflection_text.3:
After 129 e5 Qa2+ 130.Kh3 the black queen is on a2 with the White king on h3,
Rf5, Ng3 and the White e-pawn on e5.  The White win is the opening of the
e-file with e6–e7 and Rf8#.  As long as the queen is kept on the a-file /
on the 2nd rank it can be shuttled back and forth between the a-file and
the h-file and it can always be brought back to the e-file in time to
meet …e6.  The two immediate checks which lose the queen at once are

* 130…Qg2+ 131.Kxg2
* 130…Qh2+ 131.Kxh2

The blunder 130…Qe6+ is a check which abandons the a-file/e-file
control and lets 131.Kh4 and the Ne-h5 net go on.

The drawing waiting idea is to keep the queen on the a-file, or on the
2nd rank, so that a perpetual on the h-/g-file can be kept up and the
e-pawn can never be run.  In particular

* 130…Qa1!  the text book wait,
* 130…Qa3+  131.Kg4 Qg3+ etc.,  and by the same idea 130…Qa4, 130…Qa5,
 130…Qa6, 130…Qa7, 130…Qa8,
* the 2nd rank waits 130…Qb2, 130…Qc2, 130…Qd2, 130…Qe2, 130…Qf2

all keep the queen out of the Kh3 capture radius and allow Black to keep
the …Qh2+/Qg2+ perpetual and to meet …e6 by …Qxe6 / …Qe5.  The
canonical citation is

A Qa1

and the a-file family

B Qa7, G Qa6, I Qa8, J Qa5, K Qa4, N Qa3

is the same idea in waiting or checking form.  The 2nd rank waits

D Qf2, E Qb2, F Qd2, L Qc2, M Qe2

are the usual equivalent draws.  C Qg2 and H Qh2 are immediate losses
by Kxg2 / Kxh2, which is the reason 130…Qe6+ is the losing blunder
played in the game.
reflection_text.9:
The position after 129...Qa2+ 130.Kh3 is K h3 Ng3 Rf5 e5 vs K e8 Qa2. 
King h3 has the checks g2+,h2+ and the e6-h3 diagonal is blocked by the
rook on f5.  Qg2+ and Qh2+ are lost at once by Kxg2/Kxh2 and 130...Qe6
loses the perpetual that the position contains.

The perpetual is obtained by keeping the queen where it can be brought
back in one move to g2/h2 or to a3 on the 3rd rank and at the same
time where it never gives White a free tempo for e6 and for the
Kh4–Qh6+–Nh5 manoeuvre.  That is the second rank / a1 waiting
family.

In particular

* 130...Qa1! is the text book waiting move.  The queen stays on the
a-file, keeps the e5 diagonal and can be shuttled a1-a3 for a
permanent rank check on 3.

* Any quiet stay on the second rank keeps the queen out of the king’s
capture radius and keeps the g2/h2 perpetual alive.
130...Qb2, 130...Qc2, 130...Qd2, 130...Qe2, 130...Qf2 are all the same
idea.  Of the moves quoted in the list those are

E Qb2, L Qc2, F Qd2, M Qe2, D Qf2

and the a1 wait

A Qa1.

The immediate rank check 130...Qa3+ is the same idea in checking form,
130...Qa3+ 131.Kg4 Qg3+ etc., and is the move normally quoted as the
a-file drawing resource.  N Qa3 is therefore also a drawing
continuation.

Qg2+, Qh2+ are immediate losses by Kxg2/Kxh2 and Qe6 is the blunder
actually played.  The a-file moves Qa4–Qa8 are blocked in practice by
the tempo that White obtains for e6 once the queen is taken off the
second rank, so the clean textbook drawing family is the second-rank
waits together with Qa1, with Qa3+ the checking equivalent.  That is the
core of the consensus in the round.

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I agree with the a-file resource, but we should tighten the reasoning: several listed “a-file” moves are actually not legal because White’s pawn on a3 blocks the route from a2. So N Qa3, K Qa4, J Qa5, G Qa6, B Qa7, and I Qa8 cannot be the answer. The clean legal a-file waiting move is 130...Qa1.

Qa1 is the textbook form here. It keeps the queen off g2/h2, so there is no Kxg2/Kxh2 tactic, and it preserves the a1–h1 checking lane. After 130...Qa1, if White tries 131.Kh4, Black has 131...Qh1+ and then checks such as ...Qd1+/...Qd5+ to shuttle the king; the rook on f5 does not cover all those squares. If White tries 131.e6, the h-file check is still available, so White does not get the free coordination that occurred after 130...Qe6. Qb2/Qd2 may look similar, but they are less forcing and do not preserve the same a1–h1 lane. I would consolidate on A, 130...Qa1.

8.text:
After 129...Qa2+ 130.Kh3 the white king is on h3, the white battery is
Rf5+Ng3 and the black queen is on a2.  The diagonal a2-e6 is the
point of the defence and the only checks which are not at once lost
by Kxg2/Kxh2 are the perpetual checks on the g- and h-file.

As long as the queen stays out of reach of K h3 and N g3 and can
be brought back to the h-file in one move White never gets the free
e6-e7 break and the tries

    131.Rf8+  131...Kxf8
    131.Rxe5+ 131...Qxe5+

are met and the perpetual ...Qg2+/Qh2+ can be kept up.  Any quiet
waiting move which keeps the queen on the 2nd rank or on the a-file
in front of the a4-pawn does this.

In particular the textbook waiting move is

130... Qa1!

and it is the same idea as the second-rank waits

130...Qb2 130...Qc2 130...Qd2 130...Qe2 130...Qf2

and the a-file wait

130...Qa3

which is the move normally quoted as the drawing check.  Up to
notation these are the drawing resources in the list

* A. Qa1
* E. Qb2
* L. Qc2
* F. Qd2
* M. Qe2
* D. Qf2
* N. Qa3

Qa1 is the canonical citation.  The immediate checks 130...Qg2+ and
130...Qh2+ are lost at once to Kxg2/Kxh2 and the moves Qa4 Qa5 Qa6
Qa7 Qa8 are illegal in the actual position because the black a4
pawn blocks the a-file, 130...Qe6 being the losing blunder actually
played.

4.text:
After 129... Qa2+ 130.Kh3 the white king has left the a2–g2 diagonal and
the only winning ideas for White are the e-pawn break and the Rf5–Ng3
mating net.  The black king is still on e8 and the rook on f5 blocks the
e6–h3 diagonal, so the queen must not abandon the a2–e6 diagonal and
must not give up the perpetual on the h/g file.

The queen is on a2.  130...Qg2+ and 130...Qh2+ are immediate suicides,
130...Kxg2 and 130...Kxh2, and 130...Qe6 is the blunder actually played
in the game, because it abandons the diagonal and lets White get out of
the checks with 131.Kh4 Qh6+ 132.Nh5 etc.

As long as the queen stays on the a-file or stays on the 2nd rank it can
always be brought back to the h2/g2/h6/h7 squares in time for a
perpetual and it can always interpose on e6/e5 against e6. That is the
whole drawing family.

On the a-file the waiting moves

130...Qa1, 130...Qa3, 130...Qa4, 130...Qa5, 130...Qa6, 130...Qa7,
130...Qa8

all keep the a2–e6 control and the e-pawn shut off.  The canonical
citation is 130...Qa1 and the most natural checking wait is
130...Qa3+ 131.Kg4 Qg3+ etc.

The same idea is obtained by any quiet wait on the 2nd rank

130...Qb2, 130...Qc2, 130...Qd2, 130...Qe2, 130...Qf2

which keep the queen out of the K h3–Ng3 capture radius and allow the
usual ...Qg2+/Qh2+–Qb2/c2/... perpetual.  Up to notation these are the
drawing continuations A Qa1, B Qa7, D Qf2, E Qb2, F Qd2, G Qa6, I Qa8,
J Qa5, K Qa4, L Qc2, M Qe2, N Qa3.  In particular the textbook drawing
resource is 130...Qa1, essentially the same as the checking wait
130...Qa3+.

The two immediate checks on the 2nd rank are losing:

C. Qg2+ 130...Qg2+ 131.Kxg2 and
H. Qh2+ 130...Qh2+ 131.Kxh2

and 130...Qe6 is the losing blunder played in the game.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’m still with A, 130...Qa1. The key after 130.Kh3 is to keep the queen in the a-file/second-rank checking zone without giving White the free tempo 131.Kh4 that Qe6 allowed. Qa1 is the cleanest form: it keeps ...Qh1+ available, keeps the queen out of the rook’s immediate file, and preserves the usual perpetual resource. Moves like Qa6 or Qd2 look plausible, but they either lose a tempo or do not keep the same interposition/perpetual net. The second-rank retreats may look equivalent, but the canonical and most reliable move among the listed choices is 130...Qa1.

6.text:
After 129... Qa2+ 130.Kh3

White is Kh3 Ng3 Rf5 e5 and Black is Ke8 Qa2. The only winning
ideas for White are e6/e7 with Rg5/h5 and a mate on the f–file,
and a perpetual is obtained as long as the queen can be kept out of
the K h3 - N g3 capture net and can be brought back to the h/g-file
in time for ...Qh2+/Qg2+.

From a2 the queen can go anywhere on the 2nd rank or on the a-file.
Every quiet wait on the a-file or on the 2nd rank keeps the queen
out of Kxg2 / Kxh2 and keeps the a2–e6 diagonal / the a–h 2nd rank
shuttle available for a perpetual, e.g.

130... Qa1 131.e6 Qe5 132.Rxe5 etc. 131.Kh4 Qh1+ 132.Kg3 Qg1+ etc.

The same idea is obtained with the whole a-file family

Qa1 A , Qa3 N , Qa4 K , Qa5 J , Qa6 G , Qa7 B , Qa8 I

and with the whole 2nd-rank family

Qb2 E , Qc2 L , Qd2 F , Qe2 M , Qf2 D

all of which keep the queen on the a–file / 2nd rank, keep the
e-pawn under control and allow the ...Qh2/g2 perpetual.  The
capture 130...Qxa3 is the same a-file idea.

The two checks which are in the list are losing at once

130... Qg2+ 131.Kxg2   and   130... Qh2+ 131.Kxh2

and 130...Qe6 is the blunder actually played.  In particular the
text-book citation of the resource is

130... Qa1 !

and the equivalent waiting checks are 130... Qa3+, 130... Qb2,
130... Qc2, 130... Qd2, 130... Qe2, 130... Qf2, etc.  Up to naming
this is the a-file/second-rank drawing family; the only moves
among those quoted which do not draw are C Qg2+ and H Qh2+.

1.text:
After 129... Qa2+ 130.Kh3 the white king has left the a2-g2 line and the
only winning try that White has is the e-pawn.  The queen is on a2 and
it is still on the a2-e6 diagonal.  As long as the queen can be kept on
the a-file or on the 2nd rank it can always be brought back to a2/e2
in time to meet ... e6 with ...Qxe6 and it can always be brought back
to the h-file for a ...Qh2+/Qg2+ perpetual.  In particular the queen
can wait on the 1st rank

130... Qa1!

and after 131.e6 Qe5 132.Rxe5 etc. the e-pawn is neutralised and the
usual ...Qh1+ / ...Qg2+ checks can be repeated forever.  The same
waiting idea is obtained on the 2nd rank

130... Qb2, 130... Qc2, 130... Qd2, 130... Qe2, 130... Qf2

all of which keep the queen out of the range of K h3 and N g3 and
allow ...Qa2 to be re-established on the next move, and the same
idea is the capture

130... Qxa3

which is normally written 130... Qa3.  The pawn on a3 blocks the
a-file so that Qa4, Qa5, Qa6, Qa7, Qa8 are illegal from a2.  Qg2+ and
Qh2+ are met by Kxg2 and Kxh2 and Qe6 is the abandonment of the
a-file/e-file control which lets White get the e6-Rf8 mating net.
The textbook citation of the resource is the a-file wait

A. Qa1

which is essentially equivalent to the 2nd-rank waits E. Qb2, L. Qc2,
F. Qd2, M. Qe2, D. Qf2 and to the capture N. Qa3, all of which keep
the perpetual and draw.  The a-file pushes B. Qa7, G. Qa6, I. Qa8,
J. Qa5, K. Qa4 are illegal on account of the black pawn on a3, and
C. Qg2 and H. Qh2 lose the queen at once.

9.text:
After 129...Qa2+ 130.Kh3 the white king is already out of the a2–g2 diagonal
and the only real White winning tries are e6 and Rf8+. The e6 pawn push and
the Rf8+ check are both harmless as long as the queen can be brought back
on to the 2nd rank in one move for ...Qg2+ / ...Qh2+ and can be shuttled
up and down the a-file / 2nd rank without giving White a free tempo for
Kh4–Qh6+–Nh5.

The queen is therefore only safe on the 2nd rank and on a1.  On a1 it
keeps the a1–e5 diagonal and the perpetual ...Qg2+/...Qh2+ is preserved.
Any quiet wait on the 2nd rank keeps the queen out of the K h3–N g3
capture radius and keeps the perpetual alive.  

* 130...Qa1! is the textbook waiting move,

and the same idea is obtained with the second rank waits

130...Qb2 130...Qc2 130...Qd2 130...Qe2 130...Qf2

and with the checking equivalent on the a-file

130...Qa3+  131.Kg4 Qg3+  etc.

In the list this is

A Qa1, E Qb2, L Qc2, F Qd2, M Qe2, D Qf2

and the checking form N Qa3.  Qg2+ and Qh2+ are immediate losses by
Kxg2 / Kxh2, Qe6 is the blunder actually played, and the a-file moves
Qa4–Qa8 are blocked by the ...a3 pawn that now stands on a3.  Qa1 is the
normally quoted canonical drawing resource.

5.text:
After 129.e5 Qa2+ 130.Kh3 the white king is on h3, White has Rf5
Ng3 e5 and Black has Ke8 Qa2 with the Black a-pawn on a3 in front of
the queen.

The queen is on the checking rank a2–g2 and on the diagonal a2–e6.
If the queen leaves the a2–e6 diagonal White gets e6 for free and
Rf5+Ng3 becomes decisive, the move that was actually played
130…Qe6 abandons the diagonal and is the losing blunder.

The queen can stay out of K h3× and out of N g3× by staying on the
second rank or by going back to a1.  The text book waiting move is

130… Qa1!

and the same perpetual is kept by any safe wait on the second rank.
From a2 the upward a-file is blocked by Black’s own …a3 pawn so that

Qa3+, Qa4, Qa5, Qa6, Qa7, Qa8

are illegal.  Qg2+ and Qh2+ are K×g2 / K×h2 at once and 130…Qe2 is
Nxe2.  In practice the second rank waits

Qb2, Qc2, Qd2, Qf2

are the same idea as Qa1, the canonical citation being Qa1.  This is
the a-file/second-rank perpetual that Nepo missed.

2.text:
After 129... Qa2+ 130.Kh3 White's only winning material is Rf5+N g3.
The Rf5 blocks the e6-h3 diagonal and the king is now off the a2-g2
line.  As long as the queen can be brought back at will to g2/h2 the
position is a perpetual, and the queen can be kept out of the K h3 / N g3
capture net by staying on the 2nd rank / on the a-file.

From a2 the queen can therefore wait on

* a1, b2, c2, d2, e2, f2

and be shuttled back to h2/g2 whenever White tries to improve the
Rf5-Ng3 battery.  The waiting move which is normally quoted is the
a-file wait

130... Qa1!

which keeps the queen on the a-file / 2nd rank, keeps the e-pawn
under control and restores ...Qh1+/...Qg1+ etc.  The same perpetual is
kept by the essentially equivalent second-rank waits

130... Qb2, 130... Qc2, 130... Qd2, 130... Qe2, 130... Qf2

the canonical citation being

* A. Qa1

with D. Qf2, E. Qb2, F. Qd2, L. Qc2, M. Qe2 being the same idea on the
2nd rank.  Qg2 and Qh2 are lost on the spot by Kxg2/Kxh2 and 130...Qe6
is the blunder actually played. ∎

3.text:
After 129...Qa2+ 130.Kh3 White has the only real threat e6-e7 and Rf8#
with the rook on f5 and the knight on g3.  The king can only be
checked from g2-h2-h1-g4 and the diagonal g4-f5-e6-d7, so as long as
the queen can be brought back to the h-file / g-file in one move the
position is a perpetual.

The queen is still on the a2-e6 diagonal.  Any wait which keeps the
queen on the a-file or on the 2nd rank leaves White without a tempo
to play e6 with gain and leaves

...Qh2+ / ...Qg2+ / ...Qh1+

available for ever.  In particular

* 130...Qa1!

keeps the queen on the a1-e5 diagonal and at once allows
...Qh1+ and ...Qa3+ etc.  The whole a-file family is the same idea
in waiting or checking form

130...Qa3+ 131.Kg4 Qg3+ 132.Kh2 Qh3+ ... etc.
130...Qa4 ,130...Qa5 ,130...Qa6 ,130...Qa7 ,130...Qa8

and the second rank waits

130...Qb2 130...Qc2 130...Qd2 130...Qe2 130...Qf2

are the same perpetual.  e.g.

130...Qa1 131.e6 Qe5 132.Rxe5 Nxe5 etc.
130...Qa3+ 131.Kg4 Qg3+ 132.Kh2 Qh3+ 133.Kg1 Qg3+ ...

is a draw.  The two immediate checks

130...Qg2+ 131.Kxg2
130...Qh2+ 131.Kxh2

lose the queen at once and 130...Qe6+ is the losing blunder which
is actually played in the game.  The text-book citation of the
resource is

A. 130...Qa1

and N. 130...Qa3+ is the checking form of the same idea.  Up to
notation B Qa7, G Qa6, I Qa8, J Qa5, K Qa4, D Qf2, E Qb2, F Qd2,
L Qc2, M Qe2 are the same drawing waits.  C Qg2 and H Qh2 are the
immediate losing checks.

As long as the queen can be kept out of K h3× / N g3× and can be brought back to the g/h-file in one move the position is a perpetual; the a2–e6 diagonal must not be abandoned and the queen must not give up the …Qg2+/Qh2+ net.

From a2 the queen can wait on the 2nd rank or on a1. The a-file is blocked by Black’s own …a3 pawn, so Qa3+, Qa4, Qa5, Qa6, Qa7, Qa8 are illegal. Qg2+ and Qh2+ are immediate suicides Kxg2 / Kxh2. 130…Qe6 is the blunder played in the game.

Legal quiet waits:
* 130…Qa1! is the textbook citation; it keeps the a1–e5 diagonal, keeps the queen out of K h3/N g3 range and restores …Qh1+/…Qg2+ for ever.
* 130…Qb2, 130…Qc2, 130…Qd2, 130…Qf2 keep the queen on the 2nd rank out of K h3/N g3 range and keep the ...Qg2+/Qh2+ shuttle and the ...Qxe6 interposition against e6.

Qe2 is a 2nd-rank square but Ng3 attacks e2, so 130…Qe2 loses at once to 131.Nxe2; it is not a drawing wait. Qa3 is illegal because the black a-pawn stands on a3, and the same applies to Qa4–Qa8. Qg2+ / Qh2+ lose the queen to Kxg2 / Kxh2.

Hence the drawing family in the list is the canonical a-file wait

A. Qa1

and the essentially equivalent safe 2nd-rank waits

D. Qf2, E. Qb2, F. Qd2, L. Qc2

M. Qe2 is losing to Nxe2, N. Qa3 and B/G/I/J/K are illegal from a2 because of the own pawn on a3. C. Qg2 and H. Qh2 are immediate queen losses. The textbook move most often quoted is A Qa1.

9.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The position after 129...Qa2+ 130.Kh3 is White Kh3 Ng3 Rf5 e5 vs Black Ke8 Qa2. The Rf5 blocks the e6-h3 diagonal so the king can only be checked from g2/h2/h1. The only way to keep the perpetual alive is to keep the queen within one queen move of a checking square on the g/h file and to keep the e-pawn under control.

Qg2+ and Qh2+ are immediate losses by Kxg2 / Kxh2 and 130...Qe6 is the blunder actually played. The queen on a2 can reach g2/h2 in one move along the 2nd rank and can be shuttled back to a2 for a perpetual. Any quiet wait that stays on the 2nd rank keeps the queen out of K h3/N g3 capture and preserves ...Qg2+/Qh2+.

The canonical textbook wait is 130...Qa1! which keeps the queen on the a-file and keeps ...Qh1+ available: Qa1-h1 is a file check on the white king on h3. The checking equivalent on the a-file is 130...Qa3+ 131.Kg4 Qg3+ etc. The same perpetual is kept by the second-rank waits

130...Qb2, 130...Qc2, 130...Qd2, 130...Qe2, 130...Qf2

which all keep the queen on the 2nd rank, out of the king’s capture radius, and allow the queen to be returned to a2/g2/h2 at will and to interpose on e6/e5 against e6.

The a3 square is empty after 53.Rxa3, so the a-file is open in the current position. Moves that take the queen too far up the a-file, e.g. Qa4, Qa5, Qa6, Qa7, Qa8, lose the one-move access to g2/h2/h1 and give White a free tempo for Kh4 and/or e6. The earlier claim that the a3 pawn blocks the a-file is now corrected; the pawn was captured on 53.Rxa3 and the rook has since vacated the a-file.

Disagreement in the round concerns the a-file family Qa4-Qa8. Several colleagues listed them as drawing; a closer distance check shows they cannot give a check on g2/h2/h1 in one move and they allow White e6/Kh4 with gain of tempo. The reliable drawing family in the list is therefore

A Qa1, E Qb2, L Qc2, F Qd2, M Qe2, D Qf2, N Qa3

with Qa1 being the textbook citation and Qa3+ the checking form of the same idea. C Qg2 and H Qh2 are immediate queen losses, and Qe6 is the losing blunder played in the game.

which is essentially equivalent to the checking wait 130...Qa3+ 131.Kg4 Qg3+ etc.  The same perpetual is kept by any safe wait on the 2nd rank, e.g. 130...Qb2, 130...Qc2, 130...Qd2, 130...Qf2, and by any waiting move up the now empty a-file Qa3, Qa4, Qa5, Qa6, Qa7, Qa8. 

The a3 pawn that was on a3 after 43...a3 was captured on 53.R×a3, so a4–a8 is free now and the earlier “blocked a-file” objection is obsolete. Qa3 is legal and is the checking form of the same resource; Qa1 is the usual quoted form.

with the e-pawn break and with the Rf5–Ng3 mating net on the h/g file.
As long as Black can keep the queen out of K×g2/K×h2 and N×e2 and can
bring it back to the h/g file in one move the position is a perpetual and
e6 can never be played for free.

From a2 the queen can wait on the a1 square and on the whole second
rank.  The textbook form of the wait is

130… Qa1!

* 131.Kh4 Qh1+ 132.Kg3 Qg1+ 133.Kh2 Qh1+ …;
* 131.e6 Qh1+ 132.Kg3 Qg1+ …

and the e-pawn is never got out for free.  The same perpetual is kept by
any quiet wait on the second rank which stays out of the K h3–Ng3
capture net, viz.

130… Qb2 130… Qc2 130… Qd2 130… Qf2

E. Qb2, L. Qc2, F. Qd2, D. Qf2 are up to notation the same drawing
waiting idea as A. Qa1.  The checking form of the wait is 130… Qa3+.

130… Qg2+ 131.Kxg2 and 130… Qh2+ 131.Kxh2 lose the queen at once,
130… Qe2 is 131.Nxe2 and 130… Qe6 is the abandonment of the a2–e6
control which lets White get 131.Kh4 Qh6+ 132.Nh5 with the net that
was actually played in the game.  That is the canonical drawing
resource that Nepomniachtchi missed, normally quoted as A. Qa1.

9.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: After 129…Qa2+ 130.Kh3 White is Kh3 Ng3 Rf5 e5 f4 h4 vs Ke8 Qa2. The rook on f5 blocks the e6–h3 diagonal, so the only winning ideas for White are the e-pawn break e6–e7 with the Rf5–Ng3 battery and the h/g-file mating net. Black must stay out of K×g2 / K×h2 and N×e2 and be able to get back to the h/g file in one move to re-establish ...Qh1+/...Qg1+/...Qh2+ perpetual, and keep the a2–e6 control so e6 is not a free tempo.

From a2 the queen can wait on a1 and on the second rank. The textbook citation is the a-file wait

130…Qa1!

131.Kh4 Qh1+ 132.Kg3 Qg1+ 133.Kh2 Qh1+… and 131.e6 Qe5 132.Rxe5 Nxe5 is harmless; the e-pawn is shut down and the perpetual is restored.

Up to notation the same perpetual/waiting idea is kept by any quiet wait on the second rank which stays out of K h3/N g3 and can be returned to h2/g2 in one move:

130…Qb2 E, 130…Qc2 L, 130…Qd2 F, 130…Qf2 D.

All four are essentially the same drawing resource as A Qa1.

Illegal / losing in the actual position:
* After 53.Rxa3 the white rook now stands on a3. From a2 the queen cannot go to a3 and beyond, so Qa3 N, Qa4 K, Qa5 J, Qa6 G, Qa7 B, Qa8 I are not reachable from a2 in the position after 130.Kh3.
* 130…Qg2+ C 131.Kxg2 and 130…Qh2+ H 131.Kxh2 lose the queen at once.
* 130…Qe2 M 131.Ng3xe2 wins the queen.
* 130…Qe6 is the abandonment of the a2–e6 diagonal that lets White get 131.Kh4 Qh6+ 132.Nh5 and the decisive Rf5 mating net, the blunder actually played.

Consensus in the round is that the canonical drawing resource is A Qa1, with E Qb2, L Qc2, F Qd2, D Qf2 being equivalent second-rank waits of the same perpetual family. The far a-file pushes and the immediate checks Qg2+/Qh2+/Qe2 are not drawing, and the a-file pushes beyond a2 are illegal because the a3 square is occupied by the white rook after 53.Rxa3. Unresolved nuance is whether the question expects the single canonical citation A only or the whole drawing family A/E/L/F/D.

130... Qd2  F

I remain on **A. 130...Qa1**. The important point is that “same drawing family” is not the same as the single best/canonical answer. Colleague 7’s objection still seems decisive: Qc2 may look equivalent in a loose perpetual family, but it changes the queen’s relationship to the f5-rook/e5-pawn setup and is less forcing. It does not preserve the clean a1–e5 defensive coordination in the same way.

With **130...Qa1**, Black keeps the immediate h-file shuttle available after 131.Kh4, and the e-pawn break is not given a free tempo. That is exactly the defensive resource Nepomniachtchi missed with 130...Qe6. By contrast, if L/Qc2 were truly an equivalent drawing move, someone should be able to give a concrete line where it answers 131.e6 as cleanly as Qa1. I have not seen that.

The other candidates remain clearly worse: Qg2/Qh2 self-destruct to Kxg2/Kxh2, Qe2 drops the queen to Nxe2, and Qe6 is the actual losing blunder. So I would keep the group consolidated on the canonical answer: **A. 130...Qa1**.
public_text.10: I would stay with **A, 130...Qa1**. The most important point raised this round is Colleague 7's: Qc2 may look like a second-rank wait, but it changes the queen’s relation to the Rf5/e5 setup. The drawing resource here is not merely “any quiet second-rank move”; it is the move that keeps the immediate ...Qh1+/...Qg1+ shuttle while also preserving the defensive coverage that makes 131.e6 harmless. Qa1 is the canonical form of that wait. Qc2 may transpose in some loose family descriptions, but I have not seen a concrete line where Black re-establishes the perpetual after 131.e6 as cleanly as after Qa1. That distinction matters because the question asks for the drawing move, not the whole family. Qg2+ and Qh2+ self-destruct, Qe2 drops the queen to Nxe2, and Qe6 is the actual losing move. I’d keep the group on **A. 130...Qa1**.
